headline: Highest risk is medium: shared filesystem and runtime hooks create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways between ctx and oh-my-openagent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx reads filesystem and observes Claude Code PostToolUse/Stop events, while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks plus file surfaces. That creates a plausible default bridge where one agent can feed content the other may treat as instructions. The interaction is documented only indirectly, so uncertainty pushes severity up from low.
conditions: IF ctx consumes files or hook output produced by oh-my-openagent without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF oh-my-openagent injects MCP/hook content into a shared workspace, ctx may parse attacker-controlled instructions.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces.
Disable automatic parsing of hook output as instructions.
Add provenance labels to all inter-agent messages.
Review shared MCP registrations before launch.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization at the bridge.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch filesystem-backed data and runtime/session artifacts; oh-my-openagent also handles provider auth prompts and broad network egress. If they share a workspace or config tree, ctx can expose logs and graph data while oh-my-openagent can transmit copied content outward. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default setups, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents run under the same user profile with shared files, ctx data can flow into oh-my-openagent.
IF oh-my-openagent forwards copied workspace content to external APIs, sensitive ctx logs may leave the machine.
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers.
Move shared configs out of the common home directory.
Restrict oh-my-openagent network egress to approved endpoints.
Rotate any provider auth prompts after testing.
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx supports multiple instances and filesystem access; oh-my-openagent supports multiple instances, subprocesses, and broad network egress. If both are pointed at the same mutable workspace, they can race on files, configs, or generated artifacts. No locking mechanism is documented, so the safe choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or config directory, file races can occur.
IF either agent mutates shared state without locks, one agent can overwrite the other's changes.
mitigations: Run each agent in its own checkout.
Serialize writes with a simple file lock.
Disable concurrent edits during shared tasks.
Snapshot the workspace before multi-agent runs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code events and oh-my-openagent exposes task/message tooling, so one agent's output can become the other's input with little evidence of verification. That makes mistaken facts or malformed instructions propagate into downstream actions. Because the profiles do not show explicit autonomous side effects, medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent forwards ctx-generated summaries into task or message tools, errors can cascade.
IF ctx treats hook output as authoritative, downstream reasoning may amplify mistakes.
mitigations: Require human review before task execution.
Add a verification step between agents.
Mark inter-agent summaries as untrusted.
Limit message length and schema.
requires-engineering: implement signed, typed handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and mention logs, telemetry, session history, and provider auth prompts, but no residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented. The main compliance concern is policy drift around retained logs and auth material, which is narrower than medium because no specific regulated data class is shown. The other agent is cited because the risk is about their combined handling of shared operational data.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into shared logs or session history, retention policy mismatches become relevant.
IF provider auth prompts are stored alongside ctx audit/runtime logs, deletion/export handling may diverge.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared logs.
Document retention for both agents.
Purge auth prompts after setup.
Keep separate audit trails.
requires-engineering: map data classes to retention rules.
